hints: Focus on what calcium hydroxide provides in solution, lots of hydroxide ions that love to accept protons.
Notice that $\text{NH}_4^+$ can lose a proton to become $\text{NH}_3$, so think about what we call a proton donor.
Check oxidation numbers of N and H in $\text{NH}_4^+$ and in $\text{NH}_3$, they do not change, so rule out redox and link proton transfer to the final role.
walkthrough:
**Write what actually reacts**

Think of this simply as mixing $\text{NH}_4^+$ ions with $\text{OH}^-$ ions. The familiar lab test for ammonium ions works exactly like this.

$$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Spot the proton transfer**

The ammonium ion gives a proton ($\text{H}^+$) to the hydroxide ion. Hydroxide accepts the proton to make water, and ammonium becomes ammonia.

$$\text{NH}_4^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+$$

**Decide acid, base or redox**

A proton donor is a Bronsted-Lowry acid, and a proton acceptor is a base. Here $\text{OH}^-$ is the base, so $\text{NH}_4^+$ must be the acid.

No oxidation numbers change (N stays -3, H stays +1), so it is not oxidation or reduction.

options.A: Correct. $\text{NH}_4^+$ donates a proton to $\text{OH}^-$ to form $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. A proton donor is a Bronsted-Lowry acid.
options.B: Not correct. The base in this reaction is the hydroxide ion, $\text{OH}^-$, because it accepts the proton. Students sometimes swap the roles, but the species that gains the proton is the base.
options.C: Not correct. An oxidising agent gains electrons and causes oxidation numbers to change. Here N remains -3 and H remains +1 in $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{NH}_3$, so no redox occurs.
options.D: Not correct. A reducing agent loses electrons and causes oxidation numbers to change. There is no electron transfer here, only proton transfer, so this is an acid-base reaction, not redox.
